question: What should clinical care rely on instead of guesswork and doing things just because 'that is how we have always done it'?

options.A: Systematic inquiry
options.B: Emergency obstetric surgical procedures
options.C: Standard hospital administrative duties
options.D: Direct supervision by senior doctors

explanation: Systematic inquiry helps healthcare move away from unproven traditions, relying instead on solid evidence to guide patient care. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T1#BMP225_U1_T1_h1)

question: Why is an investigative mindset important for midwives on the ward?

options.A: It helps them question outdated routines to improve patient outcomes
options.B: It removes the need for keeping accurate labor ward records
options.C: It allows them to bypass hospital management rules easily
options.D: It guarantees automatic promotion to senior nursing posts

explanation: When midwives question old habits like unnecessary fasting or shaving, they can adopt safer, more modern practices for mothers and babies. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T1#BMP225_U1_T1_h1)

question: How is scientific research best defined?

options.A: A collection of personal opinions from experienced doctors
options.B: A quick review of daily patient attendance registers
options.C: A structured process to discover facts and minimize bias
options.D: An informal discussion among nurses during shift change

explanation: Scientific research relies on controlled methods specifically designed to keep personal opinions and bias out of the findings. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T1#BMP225_U1_T1_h2)

question: Why must scientific research follow a clear, structured method?

options.A: To eliminate the need for ethical clearance committees
options.B: So other professionals can verify and check the work
options.C: So hospital management can charge patients higher fees
options.D: To make sure the project takes a very long time to finish

explanation: Clear methods allow independent researchers to examine the steps and results, ensuring the findings are trustworthy. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T1#BMP225_U1_T1_h2)

question: What is a main goal of conducting research in midwifery?

options.A: Increasing the administrative workload of student midwives
options.B: Replacing doctors entirely during complicated surgical births
options.C: Solving practical problems in maternity and labor wards
options.D: Eliminating the need for community health sensitization

explanation: Midwifery research focuses directly on real-world challenges faced by mothers and midwives during pregnancy, labor, and the postnatal period. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T1#BMP225_U1_T1_h3)

question: A researcher studies whether a local herbal drink safely reduces after-birth bleeding. Which purpose of midwifery research does this fit?

options.A: Replacing standard nursing uniforms
options.B: Stopping all routine antenatal clinics
options.C: Validating indigenous practices
options.D: Increasing hospital admission fees

explanation: Studying local remedies to determine their safety and effectiveness falls under validating and understanding traditional care. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T1#BMP225_U1_T1_h3)

question: What does it mean when scientific research is described as 'empirical'?

options.A: It changes its core findings every single day
options.B: It depends entirely on the personal feelings of the researcher
options.C: It is based on direct observation and measurable evidence
options.D: It cannot be repeated by any other healthcare worker

explanation: Empirical research relies on hard data collected through direct observation in the real world rather than abstract guesses. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T1#BMP225_U1_T1_h4)

question: Why is it important that other researchers can repeat a scientific study and get the same results?

options.A: It ensures the original researcher makes a lot of money
options.B: It proves the findings are reliable when repeated by others
options.C: It makes writing the final bibliography much shorter
options.D: It stops patients from asking questions about their treatment

explanation: If different researchers follow the exact same steps and arrive at similar conclusions, the study's findings become much more trustworthy. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T1#BMP225_U1_T1_h4)

question: What three elements are combined in evidence-based midwifery practice?

options.A: Hospital budgets, administrative orders, and doctor schedules
options.B: Strict nursing rules, drug prices, and bed capacities
options.C: Research findings, clinical expertise, and patient preferences
options.D: Traditional beliefs, personal opinions, and guesswork

explanation: True evidence-based care brings together valid research results, the professional judgment of the midwife, and what the mother prefers. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T1#BMP225_U1_T1_h5)

question: What is a common challenge when trying to introduce new research findings into a busy hospital?

options.A: An immediate ban on all forms of antenatal drugs
options.B: The requirement to write a textbook before starting work
options.C: A complete lack of pregnant women visiting the clinic
options.D: Resistance from staff accustomed to traditional routines

explanation: Healthcare staff often resist change because they are used to doing things a certain way, requiring good leadership to introduce new evidence. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T1#BMP225_U1_T1_h5)

question: Why do midwives conduct research in clinical practice?

options.A: To replace traditional birth attendants with foreign personnel
options.B: To generate local solutions that improve maternal and newborn care
options.C: To fulfill academic requirements for university promotion only
options.D: To increase the cost of maternal health services in hospitals

explanation: Midwifery research focuses on finding evidence-based solutions to real clinical challenges faced by mothers and newborns locally. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T10#BMP225_U1_T10_h1)

question: How does evidence-based midwifery research impact the profession?

options.A: It makes clinical guidelines completely rigid and unchangeable
options.B: It reduces the total number of patients visiting primary health centres
options.C: It eliminates the need for doctors in all maternity units
options.D: It shifts midwifery from routine tasks to informed, autonomous practice

explanation: Using research evidence empowers midwives to make sound clinical decisions independently and improve overall standards of care. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T10#BMP225_U1_T10_h1)

question: Where do most practical midwifery research problems come from?

options.A: Direct observations and challenges encountered in clinical practice
options.B: Random guesses made without any connection to patient care
options.C: Strict orders given by hospital accountants during budget reviews
options.D: Personal political opinions shared on social media platforms

explanation: Clinical problems usually arise from real-world situations, gaps, or difficulties observed while caring for patients. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T10#BMP225_U1_T10_h2)

question: Which of these is NOT a typical source for finding a valid research problem?

options.A: Reading professional midwifery journals and clinical guidelines
options.B: Questioning why certain health education strategies fail locally
options.C: Noticing repeated delays in emergency obstetric referrals
options.D: Randomly inventing patient symptoms without any clinical basis

explanation: Valid research problems must be rooted in actual observations, literature, or theory, not fabricated symptoms. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T10#BMP225_U1_T10_h2)

question: What does the letter F stand for in the FINER criteria used for research topics?

options.A: Final
options.B: Formal
options.C: Feasible
options.D: Fascinating

explanation: In the FINER framework, Feasible checks whether the study can realistically be carried out with available resources and time. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T10#BMP225_U1_T10_h3)

question: A student wants to study every health issue affecting pregnant women across the entire country. What is the main problem with this topic?

options.A: It is far too broad and lacks feasibility for a single researcher
options.B: It focuses on an uninteresting topic with no clinical relevance
options.C: It is completely unethical and poses physical danger to patients
options.D: It is too narrow and has already been answered definitively

explanation: Broad topics covering massive populations and regions are unmanageable and lack feasibility, requiring narrowing down. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T10#BMP225_U1_T10_h3)

question: In the PICO framework for quantitative research questions, what does the letter P represent?

options.A: Procedure
options.B: Protocol
options.C: Population
options.D: Prediction

explanation: The P in PICO stands for Population or Patient group being studied. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T10#BMP225_U1_T10_h4)

question: Why is having a clear research question essential before starting data collection?

options.A: It guarantees that the research will receive immediate international funding
options.B: It automatically proves that the researcher's initial guess is correct
options.C: It guides the entire study design and ensures relevant data is gathered
options.D: It eliminates the need for any ethical approval from the hospital board

explanation: A sharp research question keeps the study focused and prevents wasting time collecting unnecessary information. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T10#BMP225_U1_T10_h4)

question: How does a null hypothesis describe the relationship between study variables?

options.A: It proves that the intervention caused a major clinical change
options.B: It states there is no significant difference or relationship between them
options.C: It assumes the experimental group always performs better than controls
options.D: It describes personal opinions rather than measurable outcomes

explanation: A null hypothesis assumes zero difference or no relationship, serving as the baseline for statistical testing. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T10#BMP225_U1_T10_h5)

question: Which type of midwifery study is least likely to require a formal statistical hypothesis?

options.A: A clinical trial testing a new drug for reducing postpartum bleeding
options.B: An analytical survey examining the correlation between age and parity
options.C: A comparative study measuring blood pressure outcomes across two clinics
options.D: A descriptive or exploratory qualitative study exploring mothers' birth experiences

explanation: Qualitative and purely descriptive studies aim to explore experiences rather than test statistical relationships, so they use research questions instead of hypotheses. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T10#BMP225_U1_T10_h5)

question: What must happen to ensure consistency across a research proposal?

options.A: Objectives, research questions, and hypotheses must align logically
options.B: Qualitative questions must always be converted into null hypotheses
options.C: Every single variable must have at least five different hypotheses
options.D: The title must be longer than the abstract summary of the study

explanation: All parts of a study must flow together seamlessly, ensuring the questions and hypotheses directly address the stated objectives. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T10#BMP225_U1_T10_h6)

question: A student's specific objective is 'To determine if community-based workshops improve postpartum clinic attendance.' Which matching research question is most appropriate?

options.A: Do community-based workshops improve postpartum clinic attendance rates?
options.B: How many midwives are currently employed in teaching hospitals?
options.C: Why do traditional birth attendants prefer delivering babies at home?
options.D: What are the general causes of poverty in rural farming communities?

explanation: The research question must directly mirror the wording and intent of the specific objective to maintain proper alignment. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T10#BMP225_U1_T10_h6)

question: What is the primary focus of quantitative research in healthcare?

options.A: Historical origins of diseases
options.B: Numbers, counting, and measuring
options.C: Personal stories of patients
options.D: Detailed psychological traits

explanation: Quantitative research relies heavily on numerical data to measure variables and analyze trends. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T2#BMP225_U1_T2_h1)

question: Which of these clinical questions is best answered using quantitative research?

options.A: What are the deep personal fears of a woman facing a stillbirth?
options.B: How do traditional birth attendants describe their community role?
options.C: How do women emotionally feel during their first caesarean section?
options.D: What percentage of mothers attend four or more antenatal visits?

explanation: Counting percentages and tracking clinic attendance rates involves numerical data collection suited for quantitative studies. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T2#BMP225_U1_T2_h1)

question: Why do quantitative studies typically use large sample sizes?

options.A: To guarantee that zero participants drop out of the study
options.B: To make sure every single person in the country is interviewed
options.C: To allow findings to be generalized to a wider population
options.D: To eliminate the need for any statistical calculations later

explanation: Larger samples help ensure the results accurately reflect the broader community rather than just a few individuals. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T2#BMP225_U1_T2_h2)

question: What does objectivity mean in the context of quantitative research?

options.A: The findings change depending on who is reading the final report.
options.B: The personal opinions of the researcher do not alter the data results.
options.C: The participants choose which questions they prefer to answer.
options.D: The study focuses exclusively on subjective emotional feelings.

explanation: Objectivity ensures that measurements and findings remain neutral and unbiased by personal feelings. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T2#BMP225_U1_T2_h2)

question: Which research design is considered the gold standard for testing new medical interventions?

options.A: Historical record review
options.B: Randomized controlled trial
options.C: Descriptive survey method
options.D: Qualitative interview study

explanation: Randomized controlled trials provide the strongest evidence of cause and effect by actively testing interventions. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T2#BMP225_U1_T2_h3)

question: A researcher wants to see if high parity is linked to shorter labour durations without testing any new drug. What study design is this?

options.A: Clinical surgical experiment
options.B: Correlational study
options.C: Randomized controlled trial
options.D: Laboratory drug trial

explanation: Checking the relationship between two existing factors without introducing an intervention is a correlational design. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T2#BMP225_U1_T2_h3)

question: What name is given to the outcome variable that is measured in a research study?

options.A: Independent variable
options.B: Confounding variable
options.C: Extraneous variable
options.D: Dependent variable

explanation: The dependent variable represents the final outcome that changes in response to the independent variable. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T2#BMP225_U1_T2_h4)

question: In a study testing whether a new oxytocin protocol reduces postpartum blood loss, what is the independent variable?

options.A: The amount of blood lost
options.B: The age of the delivering mother
options.C: The weight of the newborn baby
options.D: The oxytocin protocol

explanation: The intervention being introduced or changed by the researcher is the independent variable. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T2#BMP225_U1_T2_h4)

question: What do inferential statistics allow a researcher to do?

options.A: Avoid calculating averages and percentages completely
options.B: Throw away confusing data points that do not fit the theory
options.C: Ensure that no human error ever occurs during data entry
options.D: Make generalizations from a sample to a wider population

explanation: Inferential statistics use sample data to draw conclusions about the broader population from which the sample was drawn. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T2#BMP225_U1_T2_h5)

question: Why is finding out if a result is statistically significant important in healthcare research?

options.A: It shows the result likely happened due to the intervention, not pure chance.
options.B: It proves that every single patient in the country was interviewed.
options.C: It guarantees that the research paper will be published immediately.
options.D: It removes all need for ethical approval in future studies.

explanation: Statistical significance helps confirm that an observed effect is real and reliable rather than a random fluke. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T2#BMP225_U1_T2_h5)

question: Why must a midwife check if a study's population matches her local clinic setting before changing practice?

options.A: Findings from one country or setting may not apply safely to another.
options.B: Journals only publish articles that use local currency measurements.
options.C: Patients refuse to take medications tested outside their home region.
options.D: Hospital management bans reading international research papers.

explanation: Differences in resources, culture, and emergency care systems mean research findings must be evaluated for local relevance. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T2#BMP225_U1_T2_h6)

question: What is the best way for a practicing midwife to use valid quantitative findings in the labour ward?

options.A: Share the numbers with patients only when they complain about care
options.B: Incorporate proven methods into everyday care to improve patient outcomes
options.C: Store the journal articles away without discussing them with colleagues
options.D: Ignore all research reports and rely purely on personal guesswork

explanation: The ultimate goal of health research is to guide clinical decisions and improve the quality of patient care. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T2#BMP225_U1_T2_h6)

question: What is the main goal of qualitative research in healthcare?

options.A: Calculating the statistical risk of a disease
options.B: Understanding human experiences and behaviors
options.C: Comparing drug dosages across large populations
options.D: Measuring exact chemical levels in the blood

explanation: Qualitative research explores the why and how of human behavior instead of gathering numbers and statistics. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T3#BMP225_U1_T3_h1)

question: Why would a midwife choose a qualitative approach when studying maternal nutrition?

options.A: To calculate the exact body mass index of every pregnant woman
options.B: To measure the exact weight of food consumed daily in grams
options.C: To uncover cultural beliefs and personal reasons behind food choices
options.D: To determine the statistical probability of a deficiency disease

explanation: Qualitative methods help researchers understand the personal and cultural factors that shape how people eat and live. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T3#BMP225_U1_T3_h1)

question: Which of these is a key feature of qualitative research?

options.A: Using automated machines to measure blood pressure
options.B: Inductive analysis building themes from detailed data
options.C: Keeping the research design completely unchangeable
options.D: Testing a strict mathematical hypothesis in a lab

explanation: Qualitative studies use information gathered from people to build broad themes rather than starting with a rigid mathematical formula. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T3#BMP225_U1_T3_h2)

question: What does it mean when we say the researcher is the main instrument in a qualitative study?

options.A: The researcher must use specialized electronic laboratory equipment to test blood
options.B: The researcher remains completely invisible and detached from participants
options.C: The researcher's personal interactions and observations directly shape the data gathered
options.D: The researcher is replaced by a computer program during data collection

explanation: Because qualitative data comes from interviews and observations, the researcher's own communication skills guide what information is collected. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T3#BMP225_U1_T3_h2)

question: Which qualitative method uses a facilitator to guide a group conversation about shared community views?

options.A: Randomized controlled trials
options.B: Structured laboratory surveys
options.C: Laboratory blood testing
options.D: Focus group discussions

explanation: Focus groups bring a small group of people together to talk about a topic so the researcher can observe group opinions and shared beliefs. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T3#BMP225_U1_T3_h3)

question: A researcher wants to study how teenage mothers in a rural community feel about attending antenatal clinics. Which method best captures their personal stories?

options.A: A retrospective count of hospital beds
options.B: A closed-ended numerical questionnaire
options.C: A randomized clinical drug trial
options.D: One-on-one in-depth interviews

explanation: In-depth interviews provide a private and safe space for individuals to share sensitive personal experiences. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T3#BMP225_U1_T3_h3)

question: What is the main focus of thematic analysis in qualitative research?

options.A: Counting the exact frequency of specific words in a sentence
options.B: Measuring the physical speed at which a person reads a text
options.C: Identifying repeating patterns and codes to form broad themes
options.D: Testing a mathematical formula against numerical data

explanation: Thematic analysis involves reviewing collected data to spot repeating ideas and group them into useful themes. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T3#BMP225_U1_T3_h4)

question: How does narrative analysis differ from thematic analysis?

options.A: Narrative analysis relies entirely on laboratory blood work and numerical statistics
options.B: Narrative analysis looks at complete individual life stories rather than breaking text into codes
options.C: Narrative analysis only uses closed-ended survey questions with fixed answers
options.D: Narrative analysis avoids recording interviews and relies on memory alone

explanation: Narrative analysis keeps a person's life story in chronological order rather than chopping the text up into separate codes. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T3#BMP225_U1_T3_h4)

question: Which term describes confidence in the truth and accuracy of qualitative research findings?

options.A: Randomization
options.B: Credibility
options.C: Sample stratification
options.D: Standard deviation

explanation: Credibility means the qualitative study truly reflects the real-life experiences of the participants. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T3#BMP225_U1_T3_h5)

question: Why do qualitative researchers use 'member checking' during data analysis?

options.A: To confirm that all laboratory equipment was properly calibrated before testing
options.B: To ensure that numerical survey responses add up to exactly one hundred percent
options.C: To share preliminary findings with participants and verify that their views were interpreted accurately
options.D: To check if every participant paid their hospital membership dues on time

explanation: Member checking allows participants to look at the researcher's notes and confirm that their stories were understood correctly. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T3#BMP225_U1_T3_h5)

question: What two types of research data are combined in a mixed-methods study?

options.A: Financial data and weather data
options.B: Historical data and genetic data
options.C: Animal data and plant data
options.D: Numerical data and narrative data

explanation: Mixed-methods research specifically brings together quantitative numbers and qualitative text or stories to provide a deeper understanding of health topics. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T4#BMP225_U1_T4_h1)

question: Why is mixed-methods research useful for studying complex maternal health issues?

options.A: It completely replaces the need for traditional randomized clinical trials
options.B: It captures both measurable outcomes and human experiences behind those numbers
options.C: It requires zero funding or ethical approval compared to other designs
options.D: It guarantees that statistical results will be positive and significant

explanation: Health problems involve statistics like mortality rates alongside social and cultural beliefs, which require both methods to fully comprehend. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T4#BMP225_U1_T4_h1)

question: What is the primary focus of the quantitative part in a mixed-methods study?

options.A: Measuring variables and establishing statistical trends
options.B: Recording detailed personal life histories
options.C: Observing artistic expressions of pregnant women
options.D: Translating local dialects into English textbooks

explanation: Quantitative research relies on numbers, counts, and statistical analysis to measure specific variables. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T4#BMP225_U1_T4_h2)

question: How do qualitative findings usually support quantitative data in a mixed-methods design?

options.A: By replacing statistical errors with estimated guesses
options.B: By inflating sample sizes to meet regulatory targets
options.C: By converting narrative stories into strict mathematical formulas
options.D: By explaining the reasons behind unexpected statistical results

explanation: Qualitative data adds depth by uncovering the human context and reasons that explain what the numbers are showing. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T4#BMP225_U1_T4_h2)

question: What limitation does a purely numerical maternal mortality statistic have on its own?

options.A: It is always completely inaccurate and misleading
options.B: It cannot be printed in modern medical journals
options.C: It requires too many computers to calculate properly
options.D: It does not reveal why women delayed seeking care

explanation: Numbers show the extent of a problem like mortality, but they miss the human story and reasons behind the occurrences. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T4#BMP225_U1_T4_h3)

question: A researcher wants to study why antenatal clinic attendance is low in a rural community. Which approach provides the most comprehensive answer?

options.A: A mixed-methods study combining attendance counts with focus group interviews
options.B: A laboratory analysis of routine blood samples from local children
options.C: A purely financial audit of the clinic's monthly electricity bills
options.D: A review of international textbook definitions of rural healthcare

explanation: Combining attendance counts with interviews uncovers both the exact drop in numbers and the cultural reasons behind the low turnout. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T4#BMP225_U1_T4_h3)

question: Which mixed-methods design collects quantitative and qualitative data at the exact same time?

options.A: Retrospective longitudinal design
options.B: Convergent design
options.C: Explanatory sequential design
options.D: Exploratory sequential design

explanation: In a convergent design, both data types are gathered concurrently and then brought together during analysis. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T4#BMP225_U1_T4_h4)

question: In an explanatory sequential design, which phase comes first?

options.A: The qualitative interview phase
options.B: The literature review phase
options.C: The quantitative phase
options.D: The policy implementation phase

explanation: An explanatory design starts with numbers to spot a trend, followed by qualitative work to explain those specific findings. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T4#BMP225_U1_T4_h4)

question: What is the primary purpose of triangulation in a mixed-methods study?

options.A: Speeding up the time it takes to write a research report
options.B: Calculating the final budget for hospital equipment purchases
options.C: Comparing different data types to verify and strengthen findings
options.D: Ensuring that all research participants remain completely anonymous

explanation: Triangulation checks if quantitative results and qualitative themes match up, making the overall conclusions much more reliable. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T4#BMP225_U1_T4_h5)

question: What should a researcher do if survey numbers contradict the stories told in qualitative interviews?

options.A: Investigate the discrepancy to uncover hidden clinical realities
options.B: Abandon the research project and publish nothing at all
options.C: Change the survey numbers to match what people said in interviews
options.D: Delete all the qualitative interviews from the computer files

explanation: Contradictions between numbers and stories point to deeper complexities that require further exploration rather than being ignored. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T4#BMP225_U1_T4_h5)

question: Which of the following is NOT a common challenge for researchers in clinical settings?

options.A: Patient suspicion regarding audio recordings or surveys
options.B: Heavy clinical workloads and busy maternity wards
options.C: Infinite amounts of research funding and idle staff time
options.D: Irregular electrical power supply for electronic equipment

explanation: Clinical settings are typically very busy and underfunded, making infinite funding and idle time completely unrealistic. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T4#BMP225_U1_T4_h6)

question: A midwife researcher wants to record patient interviews in a busy clinic with frequent power outages. What is the most practical solution?

options.A: Writing down answers from memory two weeks after the interview
options.B: Waiting until a brand new power station is built
options.C: Using portable, battery-powered recording devices and keeping sessions concise
options.D: Canceling the qualitative portion of the study entirely

explanation: Battery-powered gear and short interviews bypass power failures and respect the heavy workloads of patients and staff. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T4#BMP225_U1_T4_h6)

question: What key feature should a midwife look for when reviewing a mixed-methods research paper?

options.A: A guarantee that the research cost a lot of money
options.B: The use of complex foreign words in every paragraph
options.C: True integration of both quantitative and qualitative data
options.D: An absence of any tables, charts, or statistical numbers

explanation: A good mixed-methods study goes beyond listing two methods; it integrates them to answer the research question thoroughly. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T4#BMP225_U1_T4_h7)

question: Why is it important to appraise both parts of a mixed-methods study before changing clinical guidelines?

options.A: To make sure the article was published in a foreign journal
options.B: To verify that every single patient surveyed was over forty years old
options.C: To check if the authors used the most expensive laboratory equipment available
options.D: To ensure the final recommendations are supported by solid numbers and reliable stories

explanation: Both halves of the research must be sound so that clinical changes are based on trustworthy and balanced evidence. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T4#BMP225_U1_T4_h7)

question: What is the main purpose of basic research?

options.A: To test a new drug directly on pregnant women
options.B: To expand human knowledge without immediate clinical use
options.C: To evaluate the cost of antenatal care in rural clinics
options.D: To solve an urgent hospital staffing shortage

explanation: Basic research focuses on understanding fundamental principles and mechanisms rather than solving an immediate practical problem. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T5#BMP225_U1_T5_h1)

question: Why is pure foundational research important for clinical midwifery practice?

options.A: It replaces the need for hands-on clinical training
options.B: It lowers the cost of medical equipment in labor wards
options.C: It explains the normal biological mechanisms that underpin diseases
options.D: It gives direct instructions on how to suture a tear

explanation: Understanding how the body works normally at a fundamental level is necessary before clinicians can understand and treat pathological conditions. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T5#BMP225_U1_T5_h1)

question: Which of these is a key feature of pure inquiry research?

options.A: It must show immediate financial profit
options.B: It focuses only on solving local hospital problems
options.C: It avoids laboratory settings entirely
options.D: It is primarily driven by scientific curiosity

explanation: Pure inquiry is motivated by a desire to expand knowledge and understand underlying principles rather than commercial or immediate practical goals. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T5#BMP225_U1_T5_h2)

question: Where is basic research most commonly conducted to isolate variables?

options.A: A community outreach tent
options.B: A controlled laboratory
options.C: A traditional birth home
options.D: A busy labor ward

explanation: Controlled laboratory environments allow researchers to manipulate specific variables and observe fundamental biological mechanisms without outside interference. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T5#BMP225_U1_T5_h2)

question: What is the main focus of applied research compared to basic research?

options.A: Ignoring clinical outcomes completely
options.B: Discovering universal biological laws
options.C: Solving a specific, practical problem
options.D: Working exclusively with cell cultures

explanation: Applied research takes existing knowledge and applies it to address real-world issues, such as improving patient treatments. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T5#BMP225_U1_T5_h3)

question: A researcher wants to test if a new community program lowers maternal mortality in rural clinics. What type of research is this?

options.A: Laboratory assay
options.B: Applied research
options.C: Basic research
options.D: Pure inquiry

explanation: Testing a specific intervention in a real-world healthcare setting to solve a practical problem is a clear example of applied research. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T5#BMP225_U1_T5_h3)

question: How did the medical understanding of rhesus blood group incompatibility begin?

options.A: From tracking hospital electricity failures in labor rooms
options.B: By interviewing traditional birth attendants in rural areas
options.C: Through basic immunological and physiological studies
options.D: By asking pregnant women about their dietary habits

explanation: Understanding how immune systems interact required foundational work in immunology before clinical treatments like anti-D immunoglobulin could be developed. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T5#BMP225_U1_T5_h4)

question: Which midwifery topic is a direct result of foundational endocrinology research?

options.A: How to calculate the cost of disposable delivery kits
options.B: The best way to arrange beds in a postnatal ward
options.C: The percentage of midwives working in urban health centers
options.D: How hormones alter maternal glucose metabolism during pregnancy

explanation: Endocrinology studies how hormones function in the body, which explains metabolic shifts during pregnancy. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T5#BMP225_U1_T5_h4)

question: What is the primary role of translational science in healthcare?

options.A: To replace basic research with hospital administration tasks
options.B: To fund medical equipment manufacturing companies
options.C: To train student midwives on basic anatomy charts
options.D: To connect laboratory discoveries with bedside clinical practice

explanation: Translational science takes pure knowledge gained from basic research and transforms it into practical tools and treatments for patients. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T5#BMP225_U1_T5_h5)

question: Which of these is NOT part of the journey from lab discovery to clinical use?

options.A: Clinical protocol adjustments
options.B: Phase trials and safety reviews
options.C: Immediate adoption without safety checks
options.D: Animal testing of molecular mechanisms

explanation: Scientific discoveries undergo rigorous safety testing and clinical trials before they are ever used on patients, meaning they are never adopted immediately without checks. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T5#BMP225_U1_T5_h5)

question: What is the main goal of applied research in healthcare?

options.A: To test drugs on laboratory animals only
options.B: To solve immediate, practical problems
options.C: To discover entirely new scientific theories
options.D: To increase the general knowledge base

explanation: Applied research focuses specifically on finding practical solutions to everyday challenges faced in clinical and community settings. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T6#BMP225_U1_T6_h1)

question: Why is applied research particularly valuable for midwives working in rural primary health clinics?

options.A: It prevents midwives from needing clinical guidelines
options.B: It focuses only on theoretical science without patient contact
options.C: It gives immediate answers to local maternal health challenges
options.D: It requires expensive laboratory equipment to perform

explanation: Midwives deal with practical issues daily, so research that addresses real-world clinical problems helps them improve local maternal and child health outcomes directly. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T6#BMP225_U1_T6_h1)

question: Which of the following best describes an applied research project in a maternity hospital?

options.A: Reading historical books about ancient traditional birth practices
options.B: Studying the molecular structure of human DNA in a laboratory
options.C: Testing a new way to reduce waiting times in the antenatal clinic
options.D: Discovering a brand new planet in the solar system

explanation: Improving clinic processes like waiting times is a practical, real-world issue tackled by applied research. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T6#BMP225_U1_T6_h2)

question: How does applied research differ from theoretical studies regarding immediate impact?

options.A: Applied research aims to solve current operational problems directly
options.B: Applied research takes many years before anyone can use the results
options.C: Applied research has no connection to actual patient care
options.D: Applied research is only useful for university professors

explanation: The primary purpose of applied research is to produce practical solutions that can be implemented right away to improve health services. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T6#BMP225_U1_T6_h2)

question: What is the primary focus of basic research compared to applied research?

options.A: Expanding fundamental knowledge and theory
options.B: Solving immediate problems in the antenatal clinic
options.C: Evaluating community health intervention programs
options.D: Improving local hospital management systems

explanation: Basic research aims to discover fundamental truths and expand general scientific knowledge without an immediate practical application in mind. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T6#BMP225_U1_T6_h3)

question: Which scenario represents applied research rather than basic research?

options.A: Studying the exact genetic code of a malaria parasite
options.B: Discovering a new chemical compound in a pharmaceutical laboratory
options.C: Testing if a community-based education program lowers maternal mortality
options.D: Investigating the cellular structure of human placental tissue

explanation: Evaluating a community health program to lower mortality is a practical application of research to solve a real-world healthcare problem. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T6#BMP225_U1_T6_h3)

question: What is a common topic for applied research in maternal and child health?

options.A: Studying ancient historical records of childbirth in the 1800s
options.B: Evaluating whether labor companions reduce emergency caesarean sections
options.C: Discovering new chemical elements for industrial manufacturing
options.D: Mapping out the entire human genome for future generations

explanation: Studying the effects of labor companions addresses a direct, practical aspect of maternity care and birth outcomes. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T6#BMP225_U1_T6_h4)

question: A maternity unit wants to know if a new community breastfeeding campaign increases exclusive breastfeeding rates. What type of study is this?

options.A: Pure theory
options.B: Basic research
options.C: Laboratory science
options.D: Applied research

explanation: Assessing the real-world impact of a community health campaign is a classic example of applied research. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T6#BMP225_U1_T6_h4)

question: What does research translation mean in healthcare?

options.A: Translating academic journals into foreign languages
options.B: Applying study findings to improve clinical practice and policy
options.C: Writing fictional stories based on medical textbooks
options.D: Converting handwritten notes into digital computer files

explanation: Research translation is the process of taking proven study results and using them to change policies and everyday clinical care for the better. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T6#BMP225_U1_T6_h5)

question: Why is the participation of practicing midwives important in applied research translation?

options.A: They prevent new medical technologies from entering hospitals
options.B: They are the only professionals legally allowed to write government laws
options.C: They conduct all laboratory experiments in university settings
options.D: They help bridge the gap between scientific findings and bedside care

explanation: Midwives work directly with mothers and are best positioned to implement new evidence-based practices in the maternity ward. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T6#BMP225_U1_T6_h5)

question: What defines a human subject in health research?

options.A: A medical doctor who reviews and approves institutional research protocols
options.B: A hospital patient who receives standard routine treatment without any study involvement
options.C: A living individual who provides data through intervention, interaction, or private information
options.D: Any laboratory animal used to test new pharmaceutical drugs before human trials

explanation: Human subjects refer specifically to living people from whom researchers gather data through direct contact or private records. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T7#BMP225_U1_T7_h1)

question: Why did international ethical codes like the Nuremberg Code and Declaration of Helsinki become necessary?

options.A: To reduce the financial cost of conducting large clinical trials in developing countries
options.B: To prevent future harm and protect participants after historical research abuses
options.C: To ensure that all research studies produce statistically significant positive outcomes
options.D: To speed up the process of getting new medical drugs approved by regulatory agencies

explanation: These foundational documents were created in response to severe human rights violations in past research to guarantee basic ethical protections. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T7#BMP225_U1_T7_h1)

question: What does participant autonomy mean in the context of health research?

options.A: The authority of the lead investigator to decide who qualifies for the trial
options.B: The right of individuals to make free and informed choices about participating
options.C: The obligation of researchers to pay participants a salary for their time
options.D: The requirement that all participants must complete the entire study duration

explanation: Autonomy ensures that individuals have the independent power to decide whether or not they want to take part in research. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T7#BMP225_U1_T7_h2)

question: What distinguishes undue influence from fair compensation in a research study?

options.A: Fair compensation is only provided to researchers, never to study participants
options.B: Undue influence uses excessive rewards that compromise independent decision-making
options.C: Fair compensation is illegal under international clinical trial guidelines
options.D: Undue influence always involves physical threats of violence or imprisonment

explanation: While reasonable reimbursement for time and travel is acceptable, offering excessively large rewards can pressure vulnerable people to accept risks they would normally avoid. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T7#BMP225_U1_T7_h2)

question: Which of the following represents the three core pillars of informed consent?

options.A: Information, comprehension, and voluntariness
options.B: Diagnosis, treatment, and follow-up care
options.C: Funding, staffing, and regulatory approval
options.D: Hypothesis, methodology, and conclusion

explanation: Valid informed consent strictly depends on providing adequate information, ensuring the participant understands it, and securing their voluntary agreement. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T7#BMP225_U1_T7_h3)

question: A researcher explains a complex drug trial using advanced medical terminology that the patient cannot follow. Which core pillar of informed consent is compromised here?

options.A: Information
options.B: Voluntariness
options.C: Comprehension
options.D: Confidentiality

explanation: If the participant cannot understand the terms due to jargon, comprehension fails, even if the researcher technically read out all the required facts. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T7#BMP225_U1_T7_h3)

question: What must a consent form explicitly state regarding a participant's right to leave the study?

options.A: Participants need formal approval from the hospital ethics committee before leaving
options.B: Participants can only withdraw if they find a replacement to take their place
options.C: Participants must finish the full study period to receive any financial compensation
options.D: Participants can withdraw at any time without losing their standard medical care

explanation: Participation is completely voluntary, and individuals must always be free to exit a study whenever they choose without penalty to their healthcare. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T7#BMP225_U1_T7_h4)

question: Why is it important to detail both potential risks and benefits in a consent form?

options.A: To allow participants to make a balanced judgment about whether the study is worth their time
options.B: To guarantee that every participant will experience positive health outcomes from the trial
options.C: To legally protect the research institution from ever being sued for medical negligence
options.D: To convince government regulators to approve the research budget more quickly

explanation: Full transparency about what can go wrong versus what might be gained ensures that the participant's decision is genuinely informed. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T7#BMP225_U1_T7_h4)

question: Why are certain patient groups classified as vulnerable in research contexts?

options.A: They always require emergency medical interventions during clinical trials
options.B: They lack basic literacy skills required to sign medical prescription forms
options.C: They are physically unable to travel to tertiary health institutions
options.D: Their ability to give free and unpressured consent may be compromised

explanation: Vulnerability arises when factors like poverty, illness, or hierarchical power structures make it difficult for individuals to freely say no. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T7#BMP225_U1_T7_h5)

question: What is the main ethical risk when a healthcare provider recruits their own patients for a research study?

options.A: Patients may feel pressured to join out of fear that refusing will harm their treatment
options.B: Providers will lack the medical expertise required to collect accurate research data
options.C: The hospital administration will automatically reject the research protocol
options.D: Patients will demand excessive financial compensation for participating in the trial

explanation: The dependent relationship between patients and their healthcare provider creates a power imbalance that can make participation feel mandatory rather than voluntary. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T7#BMP225_U1_T7_h5)

question: Which of the following best describes the true nature of informed consent in research?

options.A: A one-time legal document signed only at the initial recruitment interview
options.B: A final report written by the principal investigator after the trial ends
options.C: A continuous, dynamic dialogue that lasts throughout the entire study
options.D: A verbal agreement given exclusively over the telephone before data collection

explanation: Consent does not end when the form is signed; it is an ongoing communication process between researcher and participant. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T7#BMP225_U1_T7_h6)

question: A researcher discovers a new, unexpected side effect halfway through a clinical trial. What action should be taken regarding informed consent?

options.A: Immediately terminate the study without notifying any of the current participants
options.B: Keep the information confidential until the entire research project is fully published
options.C: Continue the trial normally since the original consent form was already signed
options.D: Inform all active participants about the new side effect and update their consent

explanation: Whenever new safety information emerges that could affect a participant's willingness to continue, they must be promptly informed and given the chance to re-consent. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T7#BMP225_U1_T7_h6)

question: What is the main job of an Institutional Review Board (IRB)?

options.A: Protecting the rights and safety of people in a study
options.B: Writing textbooks and publishing journals
options.C: Managing hospital budgets and buying equipment
options.D: Securing financial grants for researchers

explanation: IRBs are set up to safeguard human participants from harm and make sure their rights are respected during any research project. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T8#BMP225_U1_T8_h1)

question: Why do Nigerian health researchers need to submit their study plans to an IRB before starting?

options.A: To receive funding from the government
options.B: To get free laboratory equipment
options.C: To prove the researcher has a nursing degree
options.D: To make sure ethical standards and participant protections are met

explanation: Reviewing the plan beforehand helps ensure that any risks to participants are kept as low as possible and are worth the study's benefits. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T8#BMP225_U1_T8_h1)

question: Who represents the local community on an IRB committee?

options.A: A foreign researcher with an international PhD
options.B: A financial auditor who manages hospital accounts
options.C: A senior government minister
options.D: A layperson with no direct connection to the research institution

explanation: Community members protect local interests and help ensure the research is easy to understand and acceptable to everyday people. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T8#BMP225_U1_T8_h2)

question: Why must an IRB include both scientific and non-scientific members?

options.A: To prevent bias and provide a balanced review
options.B: To make sure everyone can run laboratory tests
options.C: To speed up drug trial approvals
options.D: To lower the running costs of the committee

explanation: Having a diverse team helps review studies from multiple viewpoints, balancing strict science with human rights and community values. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T8#BMP225_U1_T8_h2)

question: Which document always needs to be attached when submitting a research proposal to an IRB?

options.A: Informed consent forms for the participants
options.B: Receipts for ward equipment
options.C: A letter of recommendation from a national leader
options.D: Personal bank statements of the lead researcher

explanation: Consent forms are essential because the IRB must check how participants will be informed and how their agreement will be secured. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T8#BMP225_U1_T8_h3)

question: A midwife submits a study proposal on postpartum depression but forgets to include the questionnaires and consent forms. What will the IRB likely do?

options.A: Collect the data for the midwife to save time
options.B: Approve the research immediately because the topic is important
options.C: Reject the study permanently
options.D: Ask for the missing documents before doing a full review

explanation: An IRB cannot properly evaluate a study without seeing the exact tools and consent documents that will be used with human subjects. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T8#BMP225_U1_T8_h3)

question: Which level of IRB review is needed for clinical trials that involve high-risk or invasive procedures?

options.A: Administrative review
options.B: Expedited review
options.C: Full board review
options.D: Exempt review

explanation: Studies with more than minimal risk must be discussed and voted on by the entire committee at a formal meeting. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T8#BMP225_U1_T8_h4)

question: What does an 'Exempt' status mean when submitting an IRB protocol?

options.A: The study does not need to protect participant privacy
options.B: The study involves very low risk and goes through a simplified process
options.C: The board will pay a grant to the researcher
options.D: The researcher ignores national health laws

explanation: Exempt research poses minimal risk and meets specific criteria, allowing for a quicker and simpler review pathway. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T8#BMP225_U1_T8_h4)

question: Why are pregnant women considered a vulnerable group in health research?

options.A: They always refuse to sign consent forms
options.B: They are unable to understand medical instructions
options.C: They never benefit from medical studies
options.D: Their health status and fetal safety need special ethical care

explanation: Extra care is taken during pregnancy studies to protect both the mother and the unborn baby from unforeseen risks. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T8#BMP225_U1_T8_h5)

question: A student midwife wants to recruit patients from her own antenatal clinic for a study. What ethical issue does she need to watch out for?

options.A: Patients feeling pressured to join because she is their healthcare provider
options.B: Forgetting to check blood pressure
options.C: Losing paper questionnaires on the way to school
options.D: Not paying an administrative fee to the hospital

explanation: Patients might feel forced to join a study if they worry that saying no will affect the medical care they receive from their provider. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T8#BMP225_U1_T8_h5)

question: What must a researcher submit to the IRB when making changes to a study that was already approved?

options.A: A resignation letter
options.B: An apology letter to the community
options.C: A brand new application with double fees
options.D: An amendment application for review and approval

explanation: Any changes to an approved study need a formal review and clearance before the researcher can put them into action. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T8#BMP225_U1_T8_h6)

question: Why does an IRB ask researchers to send in annual progress reports for ongoing studies?

options.A: To collect extra filing fees
options.B: To check participant safety and look for unexpected events
options.C: To help students write their final thesis
options.D: To prove the hospital has available beds

explanation: Progress reports help the committee make sure ongoing studies remain safe and continue to protect human subjects over time. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T8#BMP225_U1_T8_h6)

question: Which ethical principle is the main reason we keep research participant information confidential?

options.A: Institutional efficiency
options.B: Financial compensation
options.C: Scientific advancement
options.D: Respect for persons

explanation: Respect for persons means honoring human autonomy and a person's right to privacy. This is the foundation of research confidentiality. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T9#BMP225_U1_T9_h1)

question: In midwifery research, why is protecting participant information a moral duty rather than just a polite gesture?

options.A: It speeds up data analysis
options.B: It guarantees international grants
options.C: It removes the need for ethical clearance
options.D: It prevents exploitation and maintains community trust

explanation: Safeguarding personal data protects vulnerable participants from harm and preserves the trust that communities place in healthcare research. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T9#BMP225_U1_T9_h1)

question: In research, what does the term 'privacy' mainly refer to?

options.A: Signing a consent form before a blood test
options.B: Storing completed questionnaires in a locked cabinet
options.C: Publishing data in a medical journal
options.D: A person's right to control access to their own body and personal space

explanation: Privacy centers on the person and their right to decide who has physical or personal access to them. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T9#BMP225_U1_T9_h2)

question: How is confidentiality different from privacy in a clinical study?

options.A: Privacy has no laws, but confidentiality is strictly enforced
options.B: Privacy only applies to men, while confidentiality applies to pregnant women
options.C: Confidentiality protects data already shared, while privacy deals with personal access
options.D: Hospital security guards handle confidentiality instead of researchers

explanation: Privacy guards the person from unwanted intrusion, while confidentiality safeguards information after it has been revealed. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T9#BMP225_U1_T9_h2)

question: What is the main goal of using pseudonymization in research data?

options.A: Publishing real participant names with survey results
options.B: Replacing names with unique codes while keeping a secure linking key
options.C: Destroying all notes immediately after an interview
options.D: Sharing raw audio recordings openly with community leaders

explanation: Pseudonymization swaps names for codes to protect identity, storing the matching key separately in case the data needs to be connected later. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T9#BMP225_U1_T9_h3)

question: A researcher finishes interviews at a rural Nigerian clinic. What is the best way to store the audio files digitally?

options.A: Saving files on a password-protected laptop with secure backups
options.B: Uploading unencrypted recordings to a public social media group
options.C: Leaving the memory card on a shared desk
options.D: Sending audio clips through a standard text message to colleagues

explanation: Using passwords and secure storage keeps digital research data safe from unauthorized viewing or theft. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T9#BMP225_U1_T9_h3)

question: Which midwifery research topic carries a high risk of social stigma if confidentiality is broken?

options.A: Routine measurement of maternal height
options.B: Obstetric fistulas and HIV status
options.C: Distribution of insecticide-treated nets
options.D: Standard antenatal clinic attendance rates

explanation: Sensitive health conditions like fistulas and HIV carry heavy social stigmas, making strict confidentiality essential for participants. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T9#BMP225_U1_T9_h4)

question: Why are focus group discussions harder to keep completely confidential than one-on-one interviews?

options.A: Researchers cannot control whether participants repeat what was said outside the group
options.B: Participants sign away their privacy rights in groups
options.C: Audio equipment breaks more often during group sessions
options.D: Ethics committees ban group discussions for health studies

explanation: While researchers promise to keep data secure, fellow group members are peers who operate outside the direct control of the research team. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T9#BMP225_U1_T9_h4)

question: What is the first critical step a researcher should take after discovering an accidental breach of confidentiality?

options.A: Blame the participants for the security slip
options.B: Destroy all remaining research files in the entire institution
options.C: Assess how much data was exposed and inform the ethics committee
options.D: Keep the incident secret to protect the university's reputation

explanation: Quick assessment and reporting to the ethics board allow the team to manage damage control and take corrective steps. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T9#BMP225_U1_T9_h5)

question: Why is honesty important when handling a confirmed data breach in a research project?

options.A: It saves the research team from writing incident reports
options.B: It legally exempts the lead researcher from fines
options.C: It guarantees participants will volunteer for future studies
options.D: It helps manage the fallout, support affected individuals, and maintain accountability

explanation: Being transparent shows responsibility, protects vulnerable participants from ongoing harm, and helps rebuild trust. [learn more](BMP225_U1_T9#BMP225_U1_T9_h5)

question: Why do a literature review before starting a new study?

options.A: To prevent repeating past work and find research gaps
options.B: To increase the total word count of the final thesis
options.C: To replace the need for collecting primary data
options.D: To prove that previous researchers were completely wrong

explanation: Reviewing existing studies ensures researchers do not waste resources investigating what is already well-established. [learn more](BMP225_U2_T1#BMP225_U2_T1_h1)

question: How does reading previous research help a student midwife choose a methodology?

options.A: It eliminates all possible biases during the data gathering phase
options.B: It automatically guarantees ethical approval from the hospital board
options.C: It shows which data collection tools worked well in past studies
options.D: It dictates the exact number of patients needed for every trial

explanation: Looking at past methods helps students adopt successful study designs and avoid past mistakes. [learn more](BMP225_U2_T1#BMP225_U2_T1_h1)

question: Which of the following is the best example of a primary literature source?

options.A: A systematic review combining ten different studies on eclampsia
options.B: A standard textbook chapter about normal newborn resuscitation
options.C: A published report of an original clinical trial on oxytocin use
options.D: A clinical guideline summary published by the ministry of health

explanation: Primary sources present firsthand data collected directly through original research rather than summarizing others. [learn more](BMP225_U2_T1#BMP225_U2_T1_h2)

question: What is the main function of a secondary literature source?

options.A: To register a new clinical trial before data collection begins
options.B: To provide raw participant interview transcripts for public use
options.C: To record daily vital signs in a hospital maternity ward
options.D: To summarize and interpret multiple primary research studies

explanation: Secondary sources bring together various primary studies to give a broad overview of a clinical topic. [learn more](BMP225_U2_T1#BMP225_U2_T1_h2)

question: What is grey literature?

options.A: Confidential patient hospital files kept in the medical records room
options.B: Outdated medical textbooks older than twenty years in a library
options.C: Reports and documents published outside traditional commercial academic journals
options.D: Academic research papers that have been rejected by peer reviewers

explanation: Grey literature includes government reports, conference papers, and policy briefs not managed by commercial publishers. [learn more](BMP225_U2_T1#BMP225_U2_T1_h3)

question: Why is searching for grey literature especially important for maternal health research in Nigeria?

options.A: It is the only way to access expensive paid articles without a subscription
options.B: Government documents contain zero risk of methodological bias or errors
options.C: Many local health policies and hospital audits are never published in international journals
options.D: International databases automatically translate all Nigerian languages into English

explanation: Crucial local data often sits in government or institutional reports rather than global academic indexes. [learn more](BMP225_U2_T1#BMP225_U2_T1_h3)

question: In the PICO framework, what does the letter 'I' stand for?

options.A: Intervention
options.B: Investigation
options.C: Incidence
options.D: Indicator

explanation: The 'I' in PICO represents the specific treatment, care practice, or test being evaluated in the study. [learn more](BMP225_U2_T1#BMP225_U2_T1_h4)

question: A midwife wants to know if delayed cord clamping reduces anemia in newborn babies compared to immediate clamping. What is the Outcome in this scenario?

options.A: Newborn anemia levels
options.B: Immediate cord clamping
options.C: Delayed cord clamping
options.D: Full-term newborn babies

explanation: The outcome is the clinical result or health status being measured as a consequence of the intervention. [learn more](BMP225_U2_T1#BMP225_U2_T1_h4)

question: What is AJOL (African Journals Online) best known for helping researchers find?

options.A: Historical nursing textbooks written in European countries
options.B: Raw financial data from international pharmaceutical companies
options.C: Government tax records for Nigerian healthcare facilities
options.D: Research published within African academic and medical institutions

explanation: AJOL specializes in increasing the visibility and access of peer-reviewed research originating from the African continent. [learn more](BMP225_U2_T1#BMP225_U2_T1_h5)

question: Why do advanced search engines use controlled vocabulary like MeSH terms?

options.A: To prevent students from downloading full-text PDF documents without paying
options.B: To ensure that only randomized controlled trials appear in any search result
options.C: To group articles about the same topic together despite different author terminology
options.D: To automatically translate foreign language articles into local Nigerian dialects

explanation: Controlled vocabularies link synonyms and variations of a term so you do not miss relevant articles. [learn more](BMP225_U2_T1#BMP225_U2_T1_h5)

question: Which Boolean operator should a student use to broaden a search and include synonyms?

options.A: WITH
options.B: OR
options.C: AND
options.D: NOT

explanation: The OR operator expands search results by looking for articles containing at least one of the connected terms. [learn more](BMP225_U2_T1#BMP225_U2_T1_h6)

question: A researcher wants articles that discuss postpartum hemorrhage but wants to completely exclude cases involving retained placenta. Which search string works best?

options.A: postpartum hemorrhage WITH retained placenta
options.B: postpartum hemorrhage OR retained placenta
options.C: postpartum hemorrhage NOT retained placenta
options.D: postpartum hemorrhage AND retained placenta

explanation: The NOT operator removes any records containing the unwanted keyword following it from the final result set. [learn more](BMP225_U2_T1#BMP225_U2_T1_h6)

question: What is the primary function of reference management software like Mendeley or Zotero?

options.A: To translate foreign research articles into English instantly
options.B: To run statistical analysis on raw clinical trial measurements
options.C: To check academic papers for plagiarism before final submission
options.D: To store citations and generate reference lists automatically

explanation: Reference managers help researchers organize their collected literature and format bibliographies without manual errors. [learn more](BMP225_U2_T1#BMP225_U2_T1_h7)

question: Why is critical appraisal a necessary step when reviewing retrieved literature?

options.A: To ensure the article was published in a journal with high subscription fees
options.B: To confirm that the authors used advanced reference management software
options.C: To reduce the total number of references required in a literature review
options.D: To check if the study's methods are sound before trusting its conclusions

explanation: Critical appraisal helps researchers identify methodological flaws and biases so weak studies are not cited as solid proof. [learn more](BMP225_U2_T1#BMP225_U2_T1_h7)

question: What is the primary purpose of conducting a literature review for a midwifery research project?

options.A: To collect blood samples from pregnant women
options.B: To discover what research already exists on the topic
options.C: To prove that previous researchers made major mistakes
options.D: To replace the need for data collection in the field

explanation: A literature review helps you find and understand existing studies so you do not duplicate work and can build on proven findings. [learn more](BMP225_U2_T2#BMP225_U2_T2_h1)

question: Why must a midwifery researcher identify gaps in previous studies during a literature review?

options.A: To prove that older midwives lacked proper training
options.B: To avoid reading articles published before the year 2000
options.C: To increase the total word count of the thesis
options.D: To show what important questions still need answers

explanation: Finding gaps in the literature justifies why your new study is necessary and what specific problem it will solve. [learn more](BMP225_U2_T2#BMP225_U2_T2_h1)

question: What does synthesis mean when writing a literature review?

options.A: Copying exact sentences from five different textbooks
options.B: Combining multiple sources to show common themes and debates
options.C: Summarizing one single article in great detail
options.D: Translating foreign research papers into English

explanation: Synthesis involves linking different studies together around shared ideas rather than just listing summaries one by one. [learn more](BMP225_U2_T2#BMP225_U2_T2_h2)

question: How should a midwife structure the synthesis of ten different research papers on postpartum hemorrhage?

options.A: Write a separate long paragraph for each author in alphabetical order
options.B: Group the papers by key themes like risk factors, prevention, and treatment
options.C: Combine all ten abstracts into one single paragraph without any changes
options.D: Focus only on the paper written by the most famous professor

explanation: Organizing by clinical themes allows you to compare what different authors say about the same specific issue. [learn more](BMP225_U2_T2#BMP225_U2_T2_h2)

question: Where should a researcher place the statement of the research gap in a literature review?

options.A: Hidden inside the reference list on the final page
options.B: At the start of the abstract before reading any articles
options.C: In the middle of the methodology section about sample size
options.D: At the very end of the review to lead into your own study

explanation: The literature review traditionally concludes by pointing out what is missing, which naturally leads into your research aims. [learn more](BMP225_U2_T2#BMP225_U2_T2_h3)

question: Which of the following is NOT a standard way to organize the body paragraphs of a literature review?

options.A: Listing every author in alphabetical order by their middle name
options.B: Comparing different methodological approaches used by researchers
options.C: Grouping studies by major clinical themes or variables
options.D: Arranging sources in a chronological timeline of discovery

explanation: Alphabetizing by middle name creates a random, disconnected list rather than a logical academic argument. [learn more](BMP225_U2_T2#BMP225_U2_T2_h3)

question: What is the main function of a theoretical framework in a research study?

options.A: To provide an established academic lens to explain study findings
options.B: To provide a list of medical equipment needed for labor ward
options.C: To calculate the exact financial cost of running a hospital clinic
options.D: To replace the discussion section at the end of a thesis

explanation: A theoretical framework uses recognized theories to help explain the underlying reasons behind your research results. [learn more](BMP225_U2_T2#BMP225_U2_T2_h4)

question: A midwife student wants to study why pregnant teenagers fail to attend antenatal clinics using a pre-existing psychological model of health behavior. What is this model called in the research proposal?

options.A: A statistical formula
options.B: A laboratory experiment
options.C: A clinical checklist
options.D: A theoretical framework

explanation: Using a pre-existing model or theory to guide a study on health behavior is known as applying a theoretical framework. [learn more](BMP225_U2_T2#BMP225_U2_T2_h4)

question: How does a conceptual framework differ from a theoretical framework?

options.A: It is only used when studying surgical procedures in the operating theatre
options.B: It is borrowed entirely from physics and chemistry textbooks
options.C: It uses complex mathematical formulas instead of written paragraphs
options.D: It is customized by the researcher to show specific variables in their own study

explanation: A conceptual framework is a visual or written map tailored specifically to the variables and relationships tested in your exact study. [learn more](BMP225_U2_T2#BMP225_U2_T2_h5)

question: In a conceptual framework diagram for a study on birth asphyxia, what do the arrows pointing from risk factors to the newborn outcome represent?

options.A: The financial budget allocated for resuscitating babies
options.B: The expected directional relationships between variables
options.C: The chronological history of midwifery practice in Nigeria
options.D: The exact order in which hospital nurses take shifts

explanation: Arrows in a conceptual framework visually show how independent variables are believed to influence dependent variables. [learn more](BMP225_U2_T2#BMP225_U2_T2_h5)

question: What is a major mistake students often make when writing a literature review?

options.A: Using too many recent articles from international journals
options.B: Writing a disconnected summary of one article after another
options.C: Reading articles written by Nigerian midwifery researchers
options.D: Including a conceptual framework diagram in the proposal

explanation: Listing article summaries without synthesis results in an annotated bibliography rather than a cohesive literature review. [learn more](BMP225_U2_T2#BMP225_U2_T2_h6)

question: Why is relying entirely on textbooks published twenty years ago considered a poor practice in a literature review?

options.A: Clinical guidelines and evidence-based practices change over time
options.B: Lecturers do not know how to read older fonts
options.C: Publishing companies stop printing books after five years
options.D: Old textbooks are too heavy to carry around the library

explanation: Midwifery care relies on current evidence, so outdated sources fail to reflect modern clinical standards and discoveries. [learn more](BMP225_U2_T2#BMP225_U2_T2_h6)

question: What is the main difference between an observational study and an experimental study?

options.A: The researcher does not assign any treatment or intervention
options.B: The study only involves newborn babies and infants
options.C: Data is collected exclusively through laboratory blood tests
options.D: Participants are monitored for exactly twenty-four hours

explanation: Observational studies rely on watching events unfold naturally without the researcher altering care or assigning specific treatments. [learn more](BMP225_U2_T3#BMP225_U2_T3_h1)

question: Why do researchers often use observational studies when looking at pregnant women?

options.A: Pregnant patients refuse to participate in any other type of study
options.B: Experimental trials take more than ten years to gain ethical approval
options.C: It is often unethical to deliberately expose pregnant mothers to unproven interventions
options.D: Government health ministries ban experimental research in maternity wards

explanation: Because pregnancy involves two lives, researchers cannot ethically assign harmful exposures or untried treatments just to test an outcome. [learn more](BMP225_U2_T3#BMP225_U2_T3_h1)

question: What is the main purpose of a descriptive epidemiological study?

options.A: To test a new surgical technique on high-risk labor patients
options.B: To assign pregnant women randomly to different dietary programs
options.C: To prove that a specific drug causes a reduction in postpartum bleeding
options.D: To document the distribution of health events and characteristics in a population

explanation: Descriptive studies focus entirely on mapping out health trends and disease patterns without attempting to prove direct cause and effect. [learn more](BMP225_U2_T3#BMP225_U2_T3_h2)

question: How do descriptive studies help local clinic supervisors and midwifery managers?

options.A: By providing legal protection against medical malpractice claims
options.B: By replacing the need to keep daily hospital delivery registers
options.C: By guaranteeing that no mothers will experience complications during birth
options.D: By identifying health needs and highlighting where resources are most required

explanation: Mapping health trends helps managers see which clinics face higher burdens of conditions like eclampsia or hemorrhage so they can direct supplies accordingly. [learn more](BMP225_U2_T3#BMP225_U2_T3_h2)

question: In a cross-sectional study, when is the data collected for both exposure and outcome?

options.A: Over a prospective ten-year period
options.B: At the exact same point in time
options.C: Before the participants become pregnant
options.D: Years after the participants have died

explanation: Cross-sectional designs look at a population snapshot, assessing exposure and outcome together during a single assessment window. [learn more](BMP225_U2_T3#BMP225_U2_T3_h3)

question: A researcher wants to find the current percentage of pregnant women with malaria in a clinic today. Which study design is best?

options.A: Randomized controlled trial
options.B: Retrospective cohort study
options.C: Cross-sectional study
options.D: Historical case-control study

explanation: To find out how many people have a condition at this exact moment without following them over time, a cross-sectional survey is the correct choice. [learn more](BMP225_U2_T3#BMP225_U2_T3_h3)

question: In what direction do case-control studies look when investigating a health condition?

options.A: Forward from the exposure to future outcomes
options.B: Backward from the outcome to past exposures
options.C: Outward from the hospital to the entire community
options.D: Downward from national statistics to local clinics

explanation: Case-control studies begin by selecting people with the condition and looking back into their history to find out what exposures they experienced. [learn more](BMP225_U2_T3#BMP225_U2_T3_h4)

question: Why is a case-control design useful for studying very rare birth complications?

options.A: Researchers do not have to wait years for thousands of normal births to find a few cases
options.B: Hospitals keep electronic records that completely prevent any missing data
options.C: It eliminates all possible errors related to patient memory
options.D: It guarantees that every participating mother will recover fully from the illness

explanation: Because rare conditions happen infrequently, starting with patients who already have the condition saves time and resources compared to tracking thousands of healthy people. [learn more](BMP225_U2_T3#BMP225_U2_T3_h4)

question: What is the key direction of a cohort study?

options.A: It collects data only at one single afternoon clinic
options.B: It goes backward from disease status to past history
options.C: It changes treatment protocols halfway through the year
options.D: It follows participants forward from exposure to outcome
